---
title: "Plexus"
resources:
  - gallery/
---

We introduce **Plexus**, a typed intermediate representation for biological
mechanisms. Rather than defining yet another simulator, Plexus defines a common
language whose primary objects are **biological operators**. Every operator specifies
the biological entities it acts upon, the states it requires, the relations between
these entities, and one or more numerical implementations. The Plexus research program
has three objectives. First, to define an **algebra of biological operators**. Second,
to **decompose the existing corpus** of simulation models into this common language.
Third, to construct **differentiable implementations** of these operators so that
mechanistic models can be directly inferred from biological data.

Just as compilers separate programming languages from their implementations
through an **intermediate representation**, Plexus separates biological mechanisms
from their numerical implementations. Every operator is defined by a **typed
signature** — *what* biological transformation it performs — and one or more
**implementations** — *how* it is numerically realized. The signature is the
biological contract; the implementation is a numerical choice.

Every operator may admit multiple implementations satisfying the same signature: a
mechanical interaction by Material Point Methods, finite elements, vertex or
phase-field models; a signalling operator by Hodgkin–Huxley equations, Neural ODEs
or graph neural networks. Because a mechanism is stated once, independently of its
solver, existing simulation frameworks become **complementary backends** implementing
a common intermediate representation rather than competing modelling paradigms.

## Four concepts, seven operators

The language is built around four fundamental concepts: **operators**, **sets**
(collections of biological entities across scales — particles, cells, neurons,
synapses, tissues), the **states** each element carries, and **fields** (continuous
quantities defined over space — morphogens, pressure, potentials). A biological model
is a composition of operators acting on these objects.

The central hypothesis of Plexus is that a large fraction of existing biological
simulation models can be expressed as compositions of a small number of elementary
operator families. The proposed algebra consists of **seven**:

![The elementary operator algebra of Plexus. Lateral, Aggregate, Broadcast and Exchange transform biological state. Rewire modifies biological relations, whereas Divide and Die modify biological entities. Complex biological models are obtained by composing these elementary operator families.](figures/fig_ops.png){width=100% fig-align="center"}

- **Lateral** — interactions within a biological set.
- **Aggregate ↑** and **Broadcast ↓** — many-to-one and one-to-many transformations
  across biological scales.
- **Exchange** — transformations between sets and fields.
- **Rewire** — modification of relations between biological entities.
- **Divide** and **Die** — creation and removal of biological entities.

The first four families transform biological state while preserving the underlying
organization; Rewire modifies the interaction graph; Divide and Die modify the
entities themselves. The full algebra — with typed signatures and the reference
implementation — is on **[The language](language.qmd)**.

## Composing mechanisms

Biological models are expressed as compositions of elementary operators. Plexus
represents a model as an ordered sequence of operator applications — a **schedule** —
specifying both the order and the frequency with which operators are evaluated.
Formally, one simulation step is the composition
$\Phi = \mathcal{O}_n \circ \cdots \circ \mathcal{O}_1$, whose repeated application
generates the system dynamics $x_{t+1}=\Phi(x_t)$. Different operators may evolve on
different time scales — mechanical interactions every step, diffusion, growth or
division less often — so a model is a *multi-rate* composition of biological
mechanisms rather than a monolithic solver.

Operators are **pure** transformations: rather than modifying state in place, each
returns its contribution $\Delta_i$ to the system evolution, and the complete update
$\Delta = \sum_i \Delta_i$ is passed to the numerical implementation. Introducing a
new mechanism is therefore adding a new operator to the schedule, never editing the
engine — and because nothing is mutated in place, gradients propagate through the
composition and the whole rollout stays **differentiable**.

## What it looks like

Qualitatively different dynamical systems, all expressed in the same operator
language. Each clip below is a single `spec.yaml` over the identical operators and
schedule grammar — **hover (or tab to) a title to read the exact spec that generated
it.**

<h3>Interaction &amp; flocking</h3>
<p class="opk">Lateral operators over a radius neighbour graph: a per-type force law (attraction–repulsion) and the three boids rules that sum to flocking.</p>
<p class="opk-ref">Reference — attraction–repulsion and boids adapted from <a href="https://github.com/allierc/ParticleGraph">ParticleGraph</a> (Allier et&nbsp;al.); the Vicsek model after Vicsek et&nbsp;al. (1995).</p>

      <span class="sim-name" tabindex="0">attraction–repulsion<span class="sim-spec"><pre># Full match to ParticleGraph arbitrary_3_1: 3 types, 30000 particles, sigma=0.005,
# max_radius=0.075, periodic, first_derivative, dt=0.1, 250 frames. Now feasible
# because attraction_repulsion runs on a radius neighbour graph (O(E)), not dense.

  name: arbitrary_3
  seed: 0
  n_frames: 250
  dt: 0.1
  boundary: periodic

sets:
  particle:
    n: 30000
    types:
      t0: {fraction: 0.34, p: [1.6233, 1.0413, 1.6012, 1.5615]}
      t1: {fraction: 0.33, p: [1.7667, 1.8308, 1.0855, 1.9055]}
      t2: {fraction: 0.33, p: [1.7226, 1.7850, 1.0584, 1.8579]}

fields: {}

operators:
  - {op: radius_graph,         at: particle, radius: 0.075}
  - {op: attraction_repulsion, at: particle, sigma: 0.005}

schedule: [radius_graph, attraction_repulsion]

plotting:                      # render STYLE (read by plexus.plot; engine ignores it)
  background: black
  colormap: tab10
  point_size: 2.0

<h3>Turing — Gray–Scott reaction–diffusion</h3>
<p class="opk">Reaction–diffusion on the cell–cell adjacency graph (<code>graph_diffuse</code> → <code>react</code>) — Turing's two-species activator–inhibitor system, on a 2D cell disc: the coral regime, a fine maze (small χ), and a diverging activator view (high → red, low → blue, balanced → white).</p>
<p class="opk-ref">Reference — Gray–Scott and Brusselator reaction–diffusion, after their originating models.</p>

<h3>Epithelial mechanics — a true vertex model</h3>
<p class="opk">An explicit vertex model, via <b>Tyssue</b>. Unlike a self-propelled Voronoi tissue (each cell a single point), here cells are polygons that <b>share junction vertices</b>, and those junction vertices — not the cell centres — are the mechanical degrees of freedom. An area + line-tension shape energy (<code>shape_energy</code>) relaxes the mesh toward force balance, with growth, division and cell death as explicit operations on the mesh.</p>
<p class="opk-ref">Reference — the <a href="https://github.com/DamCB/tyssue">Tyssue</a> vertex-model library; active vertex model after Farhadifar et&nbsp;al. (2007).</p>
<div class="sim-gallery g3">
  <figure class="sim-card">
    <video src="gallery/tyssue_grow_divide.mp4" autoplay loop muted playsinline preload="metadata"></video>
    <figcaption>
      <span class="sim-name" tabindex="0">grow &amp; divide<span class="sim-spec"><pre>general:   # run-level settings
  name: tyssue_grow_grow_divide   # run name (-&gt; archive/&lt;name&gt;/)
  seed: 0   # RNG seed
  n_frames: 170   # number of simulation frames
  dt: 1.0   # time step (a label: the bounded-Euler relaxation is per-frame)
  boundary: free   # domain boundary (free = unbounded; border vertices are pinned)
  dim: 2   # spatial dimension
  world:   # world box size
  - 15.0
  - 16.0
sets:   # the biological SETS (Levels) of the model
  vertex:   # VERTEX set: mesh-vertex positions -- the mechanical DOF
    n: 781   # buffer size (max elements)
fields: {}   # continuous fields
operators:   # the operators to instantiate (each realises one mechanism)
- op: mesh_seed   # build the honeycomb half-edge mesh on the vertex set (frame 0)
  at: vertex   # the set this operator acts on
  nx: 11   # lattice columns (cell centres)
  ny: 12   # lattice rows
  a: 1.0   # cell spacing (sets the base cell size)
  border: 1   # rings of border cells to drop (their vertices are pinned)
  jitter: 0.15   # initial positional disorder
  p0: 3.75   # target shape index -- the rigidity knob (&lt; ~3.81 solid, &gt; ~3.81 fluid)
  seed: 0   # RNG seed
  pin_border: false
  before_frame: 1   # run this operator once, before the given frame
- op: face_growth   # growth: inflate each cell&#x27;s target area a0 each tick
  at: vertex   # the set this operator acts on
  rate: 0.006   # growth rate of the target area per frame
  p0: 3.75   # target shape index -- the rigidity knob (&lt; ~3.81 solid, &gt; ~3.81 fluid)
  every: 1   # run this operator every N frames
- op: shape_energy   # AVM shape-energy force on the vertices (bounded Euler); reads target area a0 from the cell set
  at: vertex   # the set this operator acts on
  p0: 3.75   # target shape index -- the rigidity knob (&lt; ~3.81 solid, &gt; ~3.81 fluid)
  K_A: 1.0   # area-elasticity stiffness
  K_P: 1.0   # perimeter-elasticity stiffness
  Lambda: 0.15
  Gamma: 0.05
  mu: 1.0   # mobility (overdamped)
  dt: 1.0   # time step (a label: the bounded-Euler relaxation is per-frame)
  relax_iters: 8   # inner bounded-Euler relaxation steps per frame
  eta: 0.08   # relaxation step size
  cap_frac: 0.15   # max per-step move as a fraction of mean edge (the stability cap)
- op: face_divide_line
  at: vertex   # the set this operator acts on
  ratio: 1.6   # divide a cell when its target area exceeds ratio x base
  a0_base: 0.8660254037844386   # base target area (the reset value after division)
  p0: 3.75   # target shape index -- the rigidity knob (&lt; ~3.81 solid, &gt; ~3.81 fluid)
  every: 3   # run this operator every N frames
- op: t1_transition   # reversible T1 neighbour swaps: reconnect edges shorter than l_th
  at: vertex   # the set this operator acts on
  l_th: 0.1   # T1 threshold: an edge shorter than this reconnects
  p0: 3.75   # target shape index -- the rigidity knob (&lt; ~3.81 solid, &gt; ~3.81 fluid)
  every: 2   # run this operator every N frames
- op: topo_snapshot   # record the per-tick topology so a movie can be rendered
  at: vertex   # the set this operator acts on
schedule:   # the order the operators run each frame
- mesh_seed
- face_growth
- shape_energy
- face_divide_line
- t1_transition
- topo_snapshot</pre></span></span>
      <span class="sim-cap">cells raise their target area and divide — the vertex mesh gains cells and junctions over time</span>
    </figcaption>
  </figure>

<p class="opk">Cell death as a <b>sculptor</b>, not as cleanup. Death is one of the eight elementary operator families, and it was the only one this vesicle lacked: growth inflates and division subdivides, so every mechanism it owned pushed the surface <b>outward</b>. A dying cell shrinks, sheds its neighbours through T1 exchanges until it is a triangle, and is then extruded by a T2 collapse — the sheet closing over the gap by force balance alone. Cells marked to die are drawn <b>blue</b>. Removing 71&nbsp;% of the cells leaves the surface closed, Euler&nbsp;2, with no broken face.</p>
<p class="opk-ref">Reference — apoptotic force driving epithelial folding after Monier et&nbsp;al., <i>Nature</i> <b>518</b>:245 (2015).</p>

    </figcaption>
  </figure>

    <figcaption>
      <span class="sim-name">nine dying rings</span>
      <span class="sim-cap">895 deaths in nine bands: the vesicle does not fall apart, it closes over every gap and shrinks</span>
    </figcaption>
  </figure>
  <figure class="sim-card">

      <span class="sim-cap">285 of 400 cells extruded — the topology survives, and what is left is an ellipsoid pulled from a sphere</span>
    </figcaption>

<h3>Vertex + Turing — patterning &amp; shaping a growing tissue</h3>
<p class="opk">Growth and reaction–diffusion on a deformable vertex shell: the tissue first proliferates by growth and division to a couple of thousand cells, then reaction–diffusion chemistry both <b>colours</b> the surface and <b>drives its shape</b> — each regime buckling the shell a different way.</p>
<p class="opk-ref">Reference — growth on the <a href="https://github.com/DamCB/tyssue">Tyssue</a> vertex model; reaction–diffusion coupled to a vertex-model vesicle (our Turing × vertex prototype).</p>

<h3>Vertex + MPM — an epithelium loading an extracellular matrix</h3>
<p class="opk">Two Levels, two solvers, one experiment: the <b>vertex</b> shell of the section above grows
and divides inside a <b>material-point matrix</b> (the MLS-MPM cycle below) seeded as fibres. The
epithelium is the real <code>cellfix_B_new</code> run — 200 cells to ~6,000, its own mechanics untouched
— and its apical surface is a moving boundary the fibres feel: they are dragged, splayed and put under
stress, coloured by the local volume change |J−1| so the <b>stress front</b> travelling outward from the
tissue is the thing you watch. Adding two <b>solid blocks</b> above and below breaks the symmetry:
blocked in one axis, the epithelium grows into the other two and a sphere becomes an <b>ovoid</b>. Each
clip plays the 3D view first, then a cross-section through the same plane — the monolayer is one cell
deep, the lumen is hollow, the fibres are cut where they cross, and the blocks are the grey bands.</p>
<p class="opk-ref">Reference — the epithelium is the 3D active vertex model of
<a href="https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-018-20678-6">Okuda et&nbsp;al. (2018)</a> on the
<a href="https://github.com/DamCB/tyssue">Tyssue</a> mesh; the matrix is MLS-MPM
(<a href="https://github.com/yuanming-hu/taichi_mpm">Hu et&nbsp;al. 2018</a>). The coupling and the
<code>seed_ecm</code> / <code>cell_to_ecm</code> / <code>cell_exclude_3d</code> /
<code>ecm_stress</code> / <code>plate_confine_3d</code> operators are ours
(<code>prototype/ecm</code>).</p>

  <figure class="sim-card">

<h3>Basement membrane + junctions</h3>
<p class="opk">The same tissue, with two things that were not there before. The <b>basement membrane</b>
is a sheet of nodes joined by explicit <b>crosslinks</b>, laid down outside the epithelium and tied to
it by one <b>integrin</b> spring per node — anchored to a fixed direction, so the sheet stretches as the
tissue grows instead of sliding over it. It is <b>secreted</b>: it starts with a ninth of its material
and lays down more as the surface expands, because a sphere that triples in radius needs nine times the
area covered. The <b>junctions</b> are the cell–cell contacts, each carrying its own <b>myosin</b>, which
is recruited where a junction is longer than average. Each clip plays the four panels in turn — the
whole tissue, a cross-section, the membrane alone with its crosslinks coloured by how far they are
stretched (blue slack, red at the breaking point), and the junction network alone coloured by myosin.</p>
<p class="opk-ref">Reference — the crosslinked-sheet and secretion picture follows
<a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/j.devcel.2023.01.004">Ku &amp; Bilder (2023)</a> and
<a href="https://doi.org/10.1242/dev.200456">T&ouml;pfer et&nbsp;al. (2022)</a>; junctional myosin
recruitment by tension is the standard vertex-model feedback. The
<code>seed_basement_membrane</code> / <code>basement_membrane_bond</code> /
<code>basement_membrane_secrete</code> / <code>integrin_adhesion</code> / <code>junction_myosin</code>
operators are ours (<code>prototype/ecm</code>).</p>

<h3>Continuum mechanics — MLS-MPM</h3>
<p class="opk">The same particle Level, now a material: the decomposed MLS-MPM cycle (strain → scatter → grid solve → gather) carries elastic, fluid, and granular bodies. Each clip plays the default <b>material</b> render; most also show the run coloured by <b>deformation</b> (‖F‖), then <b>stress</b>.</p>
<p class="opk-ref">Reference — the MLS-MPM solver is our PyTorch port (<a href="https://github.com/saalfeldlab/MPM_pytorch">saalfeldlab/MPM_pytorch</a>) of Yuanming&nbsp;Hu’s <a href="https://github.com/yuanming-hu/taichi_mpm">taichi_mpm</a>, implementing MLS-MPM (Hu et&nbsp;al. 2018).</p>
<div class="sim-gallery g3">
  <figure class="sim-card">
    <video src="gallery/material_multi.mp4" autoplay loop muted playsinline preload="metadata"></video>
    <figcaption>
      <span class="sim-name" tabindex="0">multi-material<span class="sim-spec"><pre># mpm3d_multimaterial -- three materials side by side in one 3D box (the spirit of
# MPM_pytorch&#x27;s multimaterial_1_3D, trimmed to three blocks for a quick inspect):
# an elastic jelly cube, a liquid water cube and a plastic snow cube fall together.
# Three cells, one material type each (assigned by `fraction`), each block-filled.
# Tests multi-object / multi-material 3D in a single grid solve.
general: {name: material_3d_multimaterial, seed: 0, n_frames: 360, dt: 0.0032, boundary: wall, dim: 3, world: [1.0, 1.0, 1.0]}
sets:
  cell:
    n: 3
    start: [[0.24, 0.6, 0.5], [0.5, 0.6, 0.5], [0.76, 0.6, 0.5]]
    types:
      jelly: {fraction: 0.3334, youngs: 260, block: [0.14, 0.50, 0.40, 0.34, 0.72, 0.60]}
      water:
        fraction: 0.3333
        youngs: 200
        block: [0.40, 0.50, 0.40, 0.60, 0.72, 0.60]
        layers: [{frac: 1.0, youngs: 200, material: liquid}]
      snow:
        fraction: 0.3333
        youngs: 90
        block: [0.66, 0.50, 0.40, 0.86, 0.72, 0.60]
        layers: [{frac: 1.0, youngs: 90, material: snow}]
  mpm_particle: {parent: cell, per_parent: 6000, radius: 0.16, density: 1.0}
fields:
  mpm_grid: {frame: mpm_grid, n_grid: 64}
operators:
- {op: aggregate, at: cell}
- {op: gravity, at: cell, g: 16.0}
- {op: mpm_strain, at: mpm_particle}
- {op: mpm_scatter, at: mpm_particle, to: mpm_grid, drag: 0.05, a_max: 200}
- {op: mpm_grid_update, at: mpm_grid, wall_damp: 0.7}
- {op: mpm_gather, at: mpm_particle, from: mpm_grid, wall_damp: 0.7, wall_contact: 0.04, vmax: 1000000000.0}
schedule:
- aggregate
- gravity
- {substep_dt: 0.0002, steps: [mpm_strain, mpm_scatter, mpm_grid_update, mpm_gather]}
plotting:
  background: black
  up_axis: 1
  camera_elev: 1.18
  camera_zoom: 0.0
  box_frame: true
  fps: 60
  hide_sets: [cell]
  dot_size: 1.2
  render_3d: dots
  splat_size: 2.4
  splat_res: 600
  camera_turns: 0.0
  colors: {jelly: [0.40, 0.85, 0.55], water: [0.30, 0.62, 1.0], snow: [0.95, 0.96, 1.0]}

# --- auto: video descriptions (gemma-4-12B) ---
descriptions:
  movie_mpm_particle:
    description: Initially, three distinct clusters of particles are arranged in a linear sequence along a diagonal axis. Over time, the central blue cluster begins to expand and flatten, spreading across the bottom plane of the bounding box. The green and white clusters remain relatively stationary as the blue cluster grows to encompass the area beneath them. By the final frame, the blue particles form a large, thin sheet on the floor while the green and white clusters sit atop it.
    objects: &#x27;There are three primary clusters of particles: one green, one blue, and one white. The green cluster is a compact, roughly spherical mass located on the left side of the scene. The white cluster is a similar compact, spherical mass located on the right side of the scene. The blue cluster starts as a compact sphere in the center but transforms into a large, flat, two-dimensional sheet that covers the bottom of the cube.&#x27;</pre></span></span>
      <span class="sim-cap">Exchange particle↔grid (MLS-MPM) — elastic, fluid, and granular matter in one solver</span>
    </figcaption>
  </figure>

descriptions:
  movie_mpm_particle:
    description: The simulation begins with a discrete set of colored hexagonal particles distributed
      within a 3D bounding box. Over time, these particles rapidly transition into a dense, continuous
      field of points that settle toward the bottom plane of the volume. The field exhibits complex, swirling
      patterns and turbulent structures as it evolves. Eventually, the distribution stabilizes into a
      layered, multi-colored sheet with distinct peaks and valleys.
    objects: The scene contains a collection of hexagonal particles that are initially separated and scattered
      in space. These particles are rendered in a vibrant spectrum of colors including magenta, cyan,
      green, blue, and orange. As the simulation progresses, the individual hexagons merge into a massive,
      interconnected cloud of tiny points. The final state shows a large, flat surface of points with
      varying heights and intricate, nested color patterns.</pre></span></span>
      <span class="sim-cap">a deep body of water sloshes, settles, and fills the tank</span>
    </figcaption>
  </figure>
  <figure class="sim-card">
    <video src="gallery/material_visco.mp4" autoplay loop muted playsinline preload="metadata"></video>
    <figcaption>
      <span class="sim-name" tabindex="0">viscoelastic vs elastic<span class="sim-spec"><pre># material_viscoelastic_vs_elastic -- two identical-stiffness balls dropped in 2D to compare
# the NEW `viscoelastic` (Maxwell) material against pure `elastic`.
#
#   LEFT  ball = ELASTIC (orange): fixed-corotated spring; keeps full shape memory -&gt; bounces
#                repeatedly (wall_damp 1.0 = ~no wall loss, so only the material decides rebound).
#   RIGHT ball = VISCOELASTIC (purple): same youngs, but its deformation gradient F relaxes toward
#                isotropic with time-constant `tau` -&gt; stored shear stress DECAYS -&gt; it deforms on
#                impact, dissipates energy, and bounces lower each time (fast poke = solid, slow = flows).
#
# `tau` is the relaxation time (world time units). tau -&gt; inf recovers pure elastic; tau -&gt; 0 -&gt; liquid.
# `general.dt` = sim-time per FRAME (lower for slow-mo); `substep_dt` = CFL micro-step (dt/substep_dt subs/frame).
general: {name: material_viscoelastic_vs_elastic, seed: 0, n_frames: 6000, dt: 0.0015, boundary: wall}
sets:
  cell:
    n: 2
    start: [[0.3, 0.76], [0.7, 0.76]]         # cell 0 (left)=elastic, cell 1 (right)=viscoelastic
    types:
      elastic:                                 # LEFT ball -- pure elastic reference
        fraction: 0.5
        youngs: 400
      visco:                                   # RIGHT ball -- viscoelastic (Maxwell), same stiffness
        fraction: 0.5
        youngs: 400
        layers:
          - {frac: 1.0, youngs: 400, material: viscoelastic, tau: 0.05}
  mpm_particle: {parent: cell, per_parent: 3000, radius: 0.09, density: 1.0}
fields:
  mpm_grid: {frame: mpm_grid, n_grid: 128}
operators:
  - {op: aggregate, at: cell}
  - {op: gravity, at: cell, g: 9.0}
  - {op: mpm_strain, at: mpm_particle}
  - {op: mpm_scatter, at: mpm_particle, to: mpm_grid, drag: 0.0, a_max: 200}
  - {op: mpm_grid_update, at: mpm_grid, surface_tension: 0.0, wall_damp: 1.0}
  - {op: mpm_gather, at: mpm_particle, from: mpm_grid, wall_damp: 1.0, wall_contact: 0.04, vmax: 1000000000.0}
schedule:
  - aggregate
  - gravity
  - {substep_dt: 0.0001, steps: [mpm_strain, mpm_scatter, mpm_grid_update, mpm_gather]}
plotting:
  background: black
  colors: {elastic: [0.95, 0.55, 0.2], visco: [0.38, 0.10, 0.52]}   # elastic=orange, viscoelastic=DARK PURPLE
  fps: 30                # movie playback frames/sec (NEW plotting param; lower = slower bouncing)
  movie_max_frames: 600  # keep up to 600 recorded frames -&gt; ~20 s smooth (was 120 -&gt; ~4 s)</pre></span></span>
      <span class="sim-cap">two balls, same stiffness — the elastic one (orange) rings, the viscoelastic one (purple) creeps and damps</span>
    </figcaption>
  </figure>

<h3>Stigmergy — Physarum slime (one species, a disc colony)</h3>
<p class="opk">A set of agents coupled to a scalar field: agents deposit a trail, the field diffuses and decays, agents sense and steer up it — a self-reinforcing transport network (one schedule: <code>deposit → diffuse → decay → sense → steer</code>). Here a <b>single</b> species is seeded in a disc (<code>spawn: disc</code>), so the colony stays a bounded circular web; the three differ only in turn rate and sensor geometry.</p>
<p class="opk-ref">Reference — the Physarum agent is adapted from <a href="https://github.com/SebLague/Slime-Simulation">Sebastian Lague’s Slime-Simulation</a>.</p>
<div class="sim-gallery g3">
  <figure class="sim-card">
    <video src="gallery/slime.mp4" autoplay loop muted playsinline preload="metadata"></video>
    <figcaption>
      <span class="sim-name" tabindex="0">slime (default)<span class="sim-spec"><pre># slime_default -- one species, the canonical Physarum transport network.
# The monolithic `slime` operator decomposed into 5 primitives over 1 set + 1 scalar
# field: deposit (set-&gt;field) | diffuse, decay (field-&gt;field) | sense (field-&gt;set,
# turns the heading) | glide (self-propelled move). Agents spawn in a central disc;
# stigmergy grows a self-reinforcing, coarsening network.
general: {name: slime_default, seed: 0, n_frames: 400, dt: 1.0, boundary: wall}
sets:
  cell:
    n: 12000
    spawn: disc
    spawn_radius: 0.3
    types:
      a: {fraction: 1.0, move_speed: 0.006, turn_speed: 0.45, sensor_angle: 28, sensor_dist: 0.025, sensor_size: 1}
fields:
  chemical: {frame: grid, res: 220, couples_to: cell}
operators:
- {op: deposit, at: cell, to: chemical, amount: 0.045}
- {op: diffuse, at: chemical,            rate: 0.0175}
- {op: decay,   at: chemical,            rate: 0.0006}
- {op: sense,   at: cell, from: chemical, cross: -1.0, noise: 1.0}
- {op: bounce,  at: cell}
- {op: glide, at: cell}
schedule: [deposit, diffuse, decay, sense, bounce, glide]
plotting:
  colors: {a: [0.2, 0.95, 0.65]}
  background: black
  gamma: 0.7

# --- auto: video descriptions (gemma-4-12B) ---
descriptions:
  movie_cell:
    description: A dense cloud of green particles initially forms a roughly spherical shape. Over time,
      the particles begin to organize into a complex, interconnected network of filaments. These filaments
      form a web-like structure that maintains a spherical overall boundary. The network becomes increasingly
      defined as the particles align into distinct paths.

<h3>Stigmergy — Physarum slime (many species, space-filling)</h3>
<p class="opk">The <b>same</b> schedule, but agents are now seeded <b>uniformly</b> across the field (<code>spawn: random</code>) and split into 4–8 species, each depositing and sensing its own trail channel with cross-species inhibition (<code>cross: −1</code>). That is why this row looks so unlike the discs above: instead of one bounded colony, the networks fill the whole plane and segregate into distinct interwoven colours.</p>
<p class="opk-ref">Reference — the Physarum agent is adapted from <a href="https://github.com/SebLague/Slime-Simulation">Sebastian Lague’s Slime-Simulation</a>.</p>

<h3>Strange attractors</h3>
<p class="opk">A single lateral operator rides a whole cloud along a dissipative 3D chaotic flow ẋ = f(x); a tiny seed is stretched-and-folded until the cloud <em>is</em> the attractor. Ten systems ship; six shown.</p>
<p class="opk-ref">Reference — each system cites its originating paper (Lorenz 1963, Rössler 1976, Sprott 1994, …).</p>
<div class="sim-gallery g3">
  <figure class="sim-card">
    <video src="gallery/attractor_lorenz.mp4" autoplay loop muted playsinline preload="metadata"></video>
    <figcaption>
      <span class="sim-name" tabindex="0">Lorenz<span class="sim-spec"><pre># lorenz attractor -- Lorenz (1963) convection: THE butterfly, two spiralling lobes.
# A dense `cloud` is seeded in a tiny cube inside the basin; the `attractor_flow`
# operator rides every point along dx/dt = f(x) and the chaos unfolds the seed into
# the attractor. `boundary: free` -&gt; open space (the flow is bounded by its dissipation).
general:
  name: lorenz
  seed: 0
  n_frames: 10000
  dt: 0.004
  boundary: free
  dim: 3
  world: [50.0, 50.0, 50.0]
  record_cap: 800
sets:
  cloud:
    n: 60000
    start: [0.6, 0.6, 14.6, 1.4, 1.4, 15.4]
    types:
      c: {fraction: 1.0}
fields: {}
operators:
- {op: attractor_flow, at: cloud, system: lorenz, sigma: 10.0, rho: 28.0, beta: 2.6666667}
schedule: [attractor_flow]
plotting:
  background: black
  colors:
    c: [0.24, 1.0, 0.42]
  splat_size: 1.15
  splat_res: 820
  movie_max_frames: 700
  fps: 30
  camera_zoom: 0.25
  camera_azim: 0.4
  camera_elev: 0.95
  camera_elev_end: 1.4
  camera_turns: 0.08</pre></span></span>
      <span class="sim-cap">a Lateral flow ẋ = f(x) — the Lorenz butterfly</span>
    </figcaption>
  </figure>
  <figure class="sim-card">
    <video src="gallery/attractor_halvorsen.mp4" autoplay loop muted playsinline preload="metadata"></video>
    <figcaption>
      <span class="sim-name" tabindex="0">Halvorsen<span class="sim-spec"><pre># halvorsen attractor -- cyclically-symmetric (x-&gt;y-&gt;z) quadratic flow: a fat three-armed folded knot.
# A dense `cloud` is seeded in a tiny cube inside the basin; the `attractor_flow`
# operator rides every point along dx/dt = f(x) and the chaos unfolds the seed into
# the attractor. `boundary: free` -&gt; open space (the flow is bounded by its dissipation).
general:
  name: halvorsen
  seed: 0
  n_frames: 10000
  dt: 0.004
  boundary: free
  dim: 3
  world: [16.0, 16.0, 16.0]
  record_cap: 800
sets:
  cloud:
    n: 60000
    start: [-2.35, -2.35, -2.35, -1.65, -1.65, -1.65]
    types:
      c: {fraction: 1.0}
fields: {}
operators:
- {op: attractor_flow, at: cloud, system: halvorsen, a: 1.4}
schedule: [attractor_flow]
plotting:
  background: black
  colors:
    c: [1.0, 0.62, 0.16]
  splat_size: 1.15
  splat_res: 820
  movie_max_frames: 700
  fps: 30
  camera_zoom: 0.25
  camera_azim: 0.5
  camera_elev: 0.7
  camera_elev_end: 1.2
  camera_turns: 0.4</pre></span></span>
      <span class="sim-cap">the same operator, Halvorsen flow — a folded three-armed knot</span>
    </figcaption>
  </figure>
  <figure class="sim-card">
    <video src="gallery/attractor_aizawa.mp4" autoplay loop muted playsinline preload="metadata"></video>
    <figcaption>
      <span class="sim-name" tabindex="0">Aizawa<span class="sim-spec"><pre># aizawa attractor -- a torus with an axial spike drilling through a sphere.
# A dense `cloud` is seeded in a tiny cube inside the basin; the `attractor_flow`
# operator rides every point along dx/dt = f(x) and the chaos unfolds the seed into
# the attractor. `boundary: free` -&gt; open space (the flow is bounded by its dissipation).

    types:
      c: {fraction: 1.0}
fields: {}
operators:
- {op: attractor_flow, at: cloud, system: aizawa, a: 0.95, b: 0.7, c: 0.6, d: 3.5, e: 0.25, f: 0.1}
schedule: [attractor_flow]
plotting:
  background: black

    </figcaption>
  </figure>
  <figure class="sim-card">
    <video src="gallery/attractor_sprott_b.mp4" autoplay loop muted playsinline preload="metadata"></video>
    <figcaption>
      <span class="sim-name" tabindex="0">Sprott B<span class="sim-spec"><pre># sprott_b attractor -- Sprott (1994) case B: one of the algebraically simplest chaotic flows.
# A dense `cloud` is seeded in a tiny cube inside the basin; the `attractor_flow`
# operator rides every point along dx/dt = f(x) and the chaos unfolds the seed into

<h3>Inverse-square law — self-gravity &amp; electrostatics</h3>
<p class="opk">One <code>squared_law</code> operator, two regimes: <code>law: gravity</code> (mass, always attract, all-pairs) collapses a disc into a galaxy; <code>law: coulomb</code> (signed charge, like-repel) is a plasma.</p>
<p class="opk-ref">Reference — softened self-gravity after Philip Mocz’s <em>Create Your Own N-body Simulation</em> (2020); Coulomb after <a href="https://github.com/allierc/ParticleGraph">ParticleGraph</a>.</p>
<div class="sim-gallery g3">
  <figure class="sim-card">
    <video src="gallery/inverse_square.mp4" autoplay loop muted playsinline preload="metadata"></video>
    <figcaption>
      <span class="sim-name" tabindex="0">galaxy (2D)<span class="sim-spec"><pre># spiral_galaxy (2D) -- a rotating self-gravitating disk on `squared_law` (law: gravity, all_pairs).
# Initialization is a SPEC concern (no operator): `spawn: disc` places the disc, and
# `vel_init: {mode: circular_orbit}` seeds near-circular orbital speeds v = spin*sqrt(G*M(&lt;r)/r)
# from the enclosed mass, plus an optional central point mass (`central_mass`). This replaces the
# former `disk_ic` operator -- placement lives in `spawn`, velocity in `vel_init`.
#
# TWIN of the galaxy prototype&#x27;s sweep winner bh0.5_m1_j0.06_s0.9 (N=25000, world 8, disc_R 1.5,
# central mass 0.5, disk mass 1.0, spin 0.9, jitter 0.06, softening 0.08, dt 0.004, 10000 frames).
general: {name: spiral_galaxy, seed: 2, n_frames: 10000, dt: 0.004, boundary: free, world: [8.0, 8.0]}
sets:
  star:
    n: 25000
    spawn: disc                                     # flat disc, centred in the world box
    spawn_radius: 1.5
    vel_init: {mode: circular_orbit, G: 1.0, spin: 0.90, softening: 0.08, central_mass: 0.5, jitter: 0.06}
    types: {s: {fraction: 1.0, mass: 0.00004}}      # disk mass ~1.0
fields: {}
operators:
  - {op: squared_law, at: star, law: gravity, k: 1.0, softening: 0.08, all_pairs: true, compile: true}
schedule: [squared_law]
plotting: {background: black, point_size: 1, colors: {s: [0.86, 0.9, 1.0]}, movie_max_frames: 1000, fps: 25}

## Agentic mechanistic discovery

The explicit representation of biological mechanisms transforms scientific discovery
from a parameter optimization problem into a **language exploration problem**. Because
mechanisms are explicit operators rather than simulator-specific code, they are
directly accessible to agentic systems. Plexus organizes this as three loops, each at
a different level of abstraction:

- **Loop I — Understanding.** Decompose an existing simulator into Plexus operators,
  recovering an explicit mechanistic description from opaque code.
- **Loop II — Fitting.** Fit the resulting composition to observations through its
  differentiable implementations, preserving the link between parameters and
  mechanisms.
- **Loop III — Discovery.** Read the residual: propose new operators, compare
  competing mechanistic hypotheses, and extend the algebra when existing mechanisms
  fall short.

The language itself becomes the object of discovery — new biological knowledge is a
new operator, not merely a tuned parameter.

## The operator atlas

This defines a research program with three objectives: build an **algebra** of
biological operators; **decompose** the existing corpus of simulation frameworks into
that common language; and construct **differentiable** implementations so mechanistic
models can be inferred from data. The second objective is the **operator atlas** —
existing frameworks (Chaste, CompuCell3D, Morpheus, Tissue Forge, PhysiCell, Jaxley,
BrainPy, connectome GNNs, …) treated not as rival simulators but as repositories of
reusable mechanisms, each decomposed into operators, typed signatures, and
implementations.

The atlas is also a direct test of the central hypothesis: if decomposing a broad
collection of simulators converges toward a compact, reusable vocabulary, the operator
algebra is a meaningful intermediate representation for biology; if genuinely new
families keep appearing, the language remains incomplete and must be extended. The
atlas therefore serves both as a repository of biological knowledge and as the
mechanism through which the language itself evolves.

## Read the blueprint

- **[The language](language.qmd)** — the full framework mirrored section by section:
  the four concepts, the seven-family operator algebra, numerical implementations,
  mechanistic inverse modelling, agentic discovery, and the operator atlas.
- **[Optimization](optimization.qmd)** — a slime-style foraging colony tuned end-to-end
  by a black-box search over its spec, from maze to porous-pillar navigation.
- **[Inverse problem](inverse.qmd)** — fitting a Physarum network to a target by
  gradient descent through the operators.

The full framework — numerical implementations, mechanistic inverse modelling, the
agentic loops, and the reference corpus for the atlas — is in
[`paper/plexus2.pdf`](paper/plexus2.pdf).
